blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Select and interpret words and phrases from a text with care and precision, so that every analytical point stands on evidence.

blocks.heading: Evidence
blocks.text: Evidence in analysis is the exact words from the text that show the feature a point is about; without it a point is only assertion. A claim that a writer "makes the flood feel alive" needs the words that do it, and "the river shrugged off its chains" is the proof. Evidence is not decoration at the end of a sentence: it is the thing the sentence is about.

blocks.heading: Selecting the words that matter
blocks.text: Selecting evidence means taking the shortest stretch of words that carries the feature: three words that do the work beat three lines that surround them. If the point is about a verb, quote the verb; if it is about an image, quote the two or three words that build it. Every extra word is padding a reader must re-read to find nothing in.

blocks.heading: Quotation and paraphrase
blocks.text: A quotation is the text’s own words; a paraphrase is the writer’s retelling. As evidence for a feature only a quotation will do, because the feature lives in the exact words: "shrugged off its chains" shows the personification, and "describes the water breaking free" merely asserts it. A paraphrase can be useful to set up a point, but as evidence for a feature it cannot do the job the exact words do.

blocks.heading: Interpreting a word
blocks.text: Interpreting a quoted word means saying what it means in this place and what it suggests beyond that, because a word can carry a literal sense and an attitude at once. "The shelter ‘survived’ the storm" means the shelter was still standing; the inverted commas or the analysis can add that it was expected to fail, so the word suggests an ordeal survived rather than a fact of engineering. Both parts — the meaning in place and the suggestion beyond — are the interpretation.

blocks.heading: Worked example: three words, one attitude
blocks.text: Take this sentence, written for the purpose: "Officials have promised to ‘review’ the crossing." The three words that carry the writer’s attitude are "promised to ‘review’". "Promised" implies a history of undertakings, so the reader hears an institution with a record; "review" in inverted commas suggests a process that delays rather than decides, so the reader is led to expect nothing to change. Those three words, quoted and interpreted, are worth a paragraph; the other twelve are context.

blocks.heading: Where selection meets analysis
blocks.text: The words chosen here are the raw material for the quoting and commenting taught next: the paragraph in topic 1.3.2 embeds them, and the analysis of Paper 1’s questions, taught in topics 1.4 and 1.5, stands on them. Select with the feature in mind — the verb, the image, the structural move — and the rest of the analysis has something to hold.

blocks.heading: Points with nothing under them
blocks.text: An analytical point with no words from the text to support it cannot be checked by a reader, so it carries no weight: "the writer makes the reader feel the danger" names an effect and offers nothing that produces it. The guard runs the other way too: a detail misread, and built on, sinks the answer, so check each quoted word against the sentence it came from before it carries a paragraph.
